pathway.title: SM Energy Co — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: SM Energy cut net debt by USD 1,339 million in two quarters, from USD 7,353 million at 2026-03-31 to USD 6,014 million at 2026-09-30, and trailing leverage fell from 2.79x to 1.42x over the same dates [CP-1: leverage and net debt tables; calculation 3]. The mechanism was asset-sale proceeds of USD 894 million and operating cash flow, which together redeemed the 2026 and 2027 notes at par while the revolver stayed undrawn at each quarter end [CP-1A: transaction summary]. The ratio improved partly because trailing earnings gradually absorbed more of the acquired business, so some of the decline is a perimeter effect and not debt repayment alone. The Civitas merger closed on 2026-01-30 and was equity-funded, so SM Energy's creditors face a larger company with the same unsecured senior notes and a secured revolver, not a leveraged buyout.

Liquidity is strong: cash of USD 442 million plus USD 2,498 million of undrawn revolver capacity gives USD 2,940 million, while the borrowing base of USD 5,000 million is twice the USD 2,500 million of commitments, so availability is capped by lender commitments, not by reserves [CP-1: liquidity]. The maturity ladder is USD 856 million in 2028, USD 750 million in 2029, USD 1,000 million in 2030, USD 1,350 million in 2031 and USD 2,500 million across 2032 to 2034, so the wall begins in mid-2028 and totals USD 3,956 million across 2028 to 2031 [CP-1: debt maturities]. Cash generation covers the dividends: operating cash flow less capital expenditures was USD 845 million in the nine months against USD 187 million of dividends and USD 166 million of share repurchases, leaving USD 492 million before asset-sale proceeds [CP-1: calculation 7; this module's calculation 4].

The cost of the debt stack is the main structural concern. The notes carry a weighted coupon of 7.90 percent, or USD 510.1 million of coupons a year, and the notes assumed from Civitas, USD 3,556 million at 8.375 to 9.625 percent, are the most expensive layer, with a weighted coupon of 8.85 percent [CP-1: debt schedule; calculation 2]. Trailing cash interest cover of 12.73x blends the lighter pre-merger interest burden with the post-merger burden; against run-rate coupons the cover is 8.28x, which is the better guide to the current stack. Whether the high-coupon notes can be called or refinanced early depends on indenture terms that are not supplied.

Earnings carry commodity risk. Oil was about 84 percent of Q3 2026 production revenue and the Permian Basin about half of it [CP-1A: company and operating model]. Hedges are swaps and collars through the second quarter of 2028 with prices below recent realized oil prices, so they cost cash now and cap upside, and the net derivative position is a liability of USD 460 million [CP-1A: hedging]. Operating issues also matter: oil production guidance was cut for Permian downtime on acquired assets and Uinta takeaway constraints, and lease operating cost per barrel of oil equivalent has risen every quarter since Q4 2025 [CP-1A: volume risks, cost structure]. Claims outside the debt figure include delivery commitments with up to USD 205 million of deficiency payments if nothing were delivered, liquidated damages of up to USD 64 million under a drilling agreement, and a drilling commitment management expects to be excused [CP-1: claims outside the debt figure].

Shareholder returns and governance show no creditor-adverse behaviour in the documents: the merger was paid in shares, there is no sponsor, and no debt-funded distribution, drop-down or priming appears [CP-1A: behaviour table]. Management targets about 20 percent of free cash flow after dividends for repurchases, which competes with deleveraging, though management says its leverage trajectory is part of that allocation. Legal capacity to distribute cash or add priority debt cannot be tested because the indentures and the credit agreement are not supplied.

runs.text: Strengths. SM Energy has low net leverage of 1.42x on the filed trailing basis and has shown it will use asset sales and cash flow to retire debt, with USD 1,236 million of notes redeemed at par since March from sale proceeds and cash flow (400, 419 and 417). It has no note maturity before mid-2028 and USD 2,940 million of liquidity, including a revolver that was undrawn at every 2026 quarter end. It has scale and spread across four basins, with 433.1 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day in Q3 2026 with the Permian Basin about half of revenue. Operating cash flow after capital spending funds the dividend several times over. The merger was equity-funded, and lenders reaffirmed a borrowing base of USD 5,000 million after the quarter.

Weaknesses. SM Energy remains a price taker with revenue about 84 percent oil, hedges below recent realized prices and a net derivative liability of USD 460 million. Its trailing credit metrics mix standalone and merged periods and are not covenant metrics. Interest cost is higher after the merger, as the assumed notes carry coupons of 8.375 to 9.625 percent and will keep interest above the pre-merger run-rate until they are retired or refinanced. Integration and operating execution still carry risk, with oil guidance lowered, rising unit lease operating costs and acquired-asset downtime. Off-debt commitments exist but are unquantified in part. Shareholder returns continue alongside deleveraging. The documentation behind the credit, including covenants, guarantors, indentures, ratings and a post-merger reserve base, is not in the sources.

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: On 2025-11-02 SM Energy signed a merger agreement with Civitas Resources, Inc. (10-K page:14). Stockholders approved the share issuance on 2026-01-27 and the merger closed on 2026-01-30 (Q3 page:33). Each Civitas share was converted into 1.45 SM Energy shares; 124 million shares were issued, equal to 52 percent of the enlarged share count, valued at 2.4 billion on the closing price. The purchase accounting (preliminary) shows equity consideration of 2,409, replacement awards of 29, cash of 226 and total consideration of 2,664 (Q3 page:11); the cash included 201 to repay the Civitas revolver, which released its liens, and 25 for an employee retention program (Q3 page:12). SM Energy is the accounting acquirer, the deal was a tax-free reorganization, and 18 of transaction costs were expensed in the nine months (Q3 page:10). The company assumed 4.9 billion principal of Civitas unsecured senior notes (Q3 page:18); the purchase price allocation lists senior notes assumed at a fair value of 5,090 (Q3 page:11). The Fourth Amendment to the credit agreement, signed at closing, added the Civitas subsidiaries as guarantors, extended the maturity of elected commitments to 2031-01-30, raised commitments from 2.0 billion to 2.5 billion and the borrowing base from 3.0 billion to 5.0 billion, and amended financial covenant definitions (Q3 page:17). Management reports that it actioned about 400 million of run-rate synergies against an original 200 million target (R3 page:1); this is Management Language and no synergy realization in the cash flow statement is supplied.

The divestiture and the debt actions that followed form the second leg. On 2026-02-17 SM Energy agreed to sell about 61,000 net acres in its southern Maverick Basin for 950 million of cash, with a deposit of 7.5 percent placed in escrow (10-K page:183). The sale closed on 2026-04-30 and, after a post-quarter settlement, total net cash proceeds were 894 with a gain of 260 (Q3 page:13). New debt issued in 2026: 1.0 billion of 6.625 percent Senior Notes due 2034, issued at par on 2026-03-09, with net proceeds of 984 after fees (Q3 page:20), used to fund a tender offer. The tender repurchased 894 principal of the 8.375 percent notes due 2028, at 103.175 percent of principal, for total consideration of 924, leaving 456 outstanding (Q3 page:20). Proceeds of the sale redeemed at par the 400 of 5.0 percent notes due 2026 on 2026-05-11 and the 419 of 6.75 percent notes due 2026 on 2026-06-01, and cash flow redeemed the 417 of 6.625 percent notes due 2027 on 2026-09-04 (Q3 pages:20-21). There was no new issuance after the 2034 notes in the supplied sources, and the revolver was undrawn at each quarter end. Net debt fell from 7,353 at 2026-03-31 to 6,014 at 2026-09-30 as stated in the CP-1 handoff, and management says it is on track for low one-times leverage at mid-cycle prices by year-end 2026 (R3 page:2, Management Language; the term is not defined in the sources).

Use of proceeds, liquidity effect and status are all documented for the 2034 notes, tender and redemptions. For the merger itself, no sponsor, bridge financing or new committed financing is described; the revolver was amended, not drawn. No transaction announced but not yet closed appears in the sources as of the cutoff.

fields.value: SM Energy is an independent oil and gas producer whose profile changed in one step on 2026-01-30, when it acquired Civitas Resources for stock and became a four-basin operator, then partly reversed the change by selling its southern Maverick Basin assets on 2026-04-30. For a creditor the transaction matters for four reasons. First, it was paid mainly in equity, with no sponsor and no leveraged buyout structure; the debt increase came from assumed notes, not new borrowing, and the revolver was left undrawn. Second, management used asset-sale proceeds and cash flow to retire the shortest notes and part of the highest-coupon assumed issue, so the first note maturity is mid-2028 and revolver availability is intact. Third, the operating base is oil-weighted and exposed to price, basis and takeaway constraints, partly offset by a hedge book priced below recent realized oil prices that shows as a liability. Fourth, the evidence on ownership control, legal capacity under the indentures and reserves after the merger is missing, so conclusions about willingness are supported by documented actions only, and conclusions about permissions are not drawn. The documented behaviour is deleveraging with continuing shareholder returns; no priming, uptiering, drop-down, debt-funded distribution or related-party leakage appears in the supplied text.

fields.value: On 2025-11-02 SM Energy signed a merger agreement with Civitas Resources, Inc. (10-K page:14). Stockholders approved the share issuance on 2026-01-27 and the merger closed on 2026-01-30 (Q3 page:33). Each Civitas share was converted into 1.45 SM Energy shares; 124 million shares were issued, equal to 52 percent of the enlarged share count, valued at 2.4 billion on the closing price. The purchase accounting (preliminary) shows equity consideration of 2,409, replacement awards of 29, cash of 226 and total consideration of 2,664 (Q3 page:11); the cash included 201 to repay the Civitas revolver, which released its liens, and 25 for an employee retention program (Q3 page:12). SM Energy is the accounting acquirer, the deal was a tax-free reorganization, and 18 of transaction costs were expensed in the nine months (Q3 page:10). The company assumed 4.9 billion principal of Civitas unsecured senior notes (Q3 page:18); the purchase price allocation lists senior notes assumed at a fair value of 5,090 (Q3 page:11). The Fourth Amendment to the credit agreement, signed at closing, added the Civitas subsidiaries as guarantors, extended the maturity of elected commitments to 2031-01-30, raised commitments from 2.0 billion to 2.5 billion and the borrowing base from 3.0 billion to 5.0 billion, and amended financial covenant definitions (Q3 page:17). Management reports that it actioned about 400 million of run-rate synergies against an original 200 million target (R3 page:1); this is Management Language and no synergy realization in the cash flow statement is supplied.

fields.value: The divestiture and the debt actions that followed form the second leg. On 2026-02-17 SM Energy agreed to sell about 61,000 net acres in its southern Maverick Basin for 950 million of cash, with a deposit of 7.5 percent placed in escrow (10-K page:183). The sale closed on 2026-04-30 and, after a post-quarter settlement, total net cash proceeds were 894 with a gain of 260 (Q3 page:13). New debt issued in 2026: 1.0 billion of 6.625 percent Senior Notes due 2034, issued at par on 2026-03-09, with net proceeds of 984 after fees (Q3 page:20), used to fund a tender offer. The tender repurchased 894 principal of the 8.375 percent notes due 2028, at 103.175 percent of principal, for total consideration of 924, leaving 456 outstanding (Q3 page:20). Proceeds of the sale redeemed at par the 400 of 5.0 percent notes due 2026 on 2026-05-11 and the 419 of 6.75 percent notes due 2026 on 2026-06-01, and cash flow redeemed the 417 of 6.625 percent notes due 2027 on 2026-09-04 (Q3 pages:20-21). There was no new issuance after the 2034 notes in the supplied sources, and the revolver was undrawn at each quarter end. Net debt fell from 7,353 at 2026-03-31 to 6,014 at 2026-09-30 as stated in the CP-1 handoff, and management says it is on track for low one-times leverage at mid-cycle prices by year-end 2026 (R3 page:2, Management Language; the term is not defined in the sources).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: SM Energy's credit standing is sound and improving, but it depends on oil prices and on a newly merged earnings base. The strongest support is balance-sheet strength: net debt of USD 6,014 million is 1.42x trailing adjusted EBITDAX, the revolver is undrawn, liquidity is USD 2,940 million, and no note matures before mid-2028. The weakest point is that trailing earnings blend the old and merged company, so leverage is not on a clean pro forma basis, and covenant terms, ratings and legal documents are not in the sources. The outcome will be decided by oil prices and basis through 2027, by whether free cash flow keeps funding both debt reduction and shareholder returns, and by how the USD 3,956 million of notes due 2028 to 2031 is managed.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: SM Energy cut net debt by USD 1,339 million in two quarters, from USD 7,353 million at 2026-03-31 to USD 6,014 million at 2026-09-30, and trailing leverage fell from 2.79x to 1.42x over the same dates [CP-1: leverage and net debt tables; calculation 3]. The mechanism was asset-sale proceeds of USD 894 million and operating cash flow, which together redeemed the 2026 and 2027 notes at par while the revolver stayed undrawn at each quarter end [CP-1A: transaction summary]. The ratio improved partly because trailing earnings gradually absorbed more of the acquired business, so some of the decline is a perimeter effect and not debt repayment alone. The Civitas merger closed on 2026-01-30 and was equity-funded, so SM Energy's creditors face a larger company with the same unsecured senior notes and a secured revolver, not a leveraged buyout.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Liquidity is strong: cash of USD 442 million plus USD 2,498 million of undrawn revolver capacity gives USD 2,940 million, while the borrowing base of USD 5,000 million is twice the USD 2,500 million of commitments, so availability is capped by lender commitments, not by reserves [CP-1: liquidity]. The maturity ladder is USD 856 million in 2028, USD 750 million in 2029, USD 1,000 million in 2030, USD 1,350 million in 2031 and USD 2,500 million across 2032 to 2034, so the wall begins in mid-2028 and totals USD 3,956 million across 2028 to 2031 [CP-1: debt maturities]. Cash generation covers the dividends: operating cash flow less capital expenditures was USD 845 million in the nine months against USD 187 million of dividends and USD 166 million of share repurchases, leaving USD 492 million before asset-sale proceeds [CP-1: calculation 7; this module's calculation 4].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The cost of the debt stack is the main structural concern. The notes carry a weighted coupon of 7.90 percent, or USD 510.1 million of coupons a year, and the notes assumed from Civitas, USD 3,556 million at 8.375 to 9.625 percent, are the most expensive layer, with a weighted coupon of 8.85 percent [CP-1: debt schedule; calculation 2]. Trailing cash interest cover of 12.73x blends the lighter pre-merger interest burden with the post-merger burden; against run-rate coupons the cover is 8.28x, which is the better guide to the current stack. Whether the high-coupon notes can be called or refinanced early depends on indenture terms that are not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Earnings carry commodity risk. Oil was about 84 percent of Q3 2026 production revenue and the Permian Basin about half of it [CP-1A: company and operating model]. Hedges are swaps and collars through the second quarter of 2028 with prices below recent realized oil prices, so they cost cash now and cap upside, and the net derivative position is a liability of USD 460 million [CP-1A: hedging]. Operating issues also matter: oil production guidance was cut for Permian downtime on acquired assets and Uinta takeaway constraints, and lease operating cost per barrel of oil equivalent has risen every quarter since Q4 2025 [CP-1A: volume risks, cost structure]. Claims outside the debt figure include delivery commitments with up to USD 205 million of deficiency payments if nothing were delivered, liquidated damages of up to USD 64 million under a drilling agreement, and a drilling commitment management expects to be excused [CP-1: claims outside the debt figure].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Shareholder returns and governance show no creditor-adverse behaviour in the documents: the merger was paid in shares, there is no sponsor, and no debt-funded distribution, drop-down or priming appears [CP-1A: behaviour table]. Management targets about 20 percent of free cash flow after dividends for repurchases, which competes with deleveraging, though management says its leverage trajectory is part of that allocation. Legal capacity to distribute cash or add priority debt cannot be tested because the indentures and the credit agreement are not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. SM Energy has low net leverage of 1.42x on the filed trailing basis and has shown it will use asset sales and cash flow to retire debt, with USD 1,236 million of notes redeemed at par since March from sale proceeds and cash flow (400, 419 and 417). It has no note maturity before mid-2028 and USD 2,940 million of liquidity, including a revolver that was undrawn at every 2026 quarter end. It has scale and spread across four basins, with 433.1 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day in Q3 2026 with the Permian Basin about half of revenue. Operating cash flow after capital spending funds the dividend several times over. The merger was equity-funded, and lenders reaffirmed a borrowing base of USD 5,000 million after the quarter.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. SM Energy remains a price taker with revenue about 84 percent oil, hedges below recent realized prices and a net derivative liability of USD 460 million. Its trailing credit metrics mix standalone and merged periods and are not covenant metrics. Interest cost is higher after the merger, as the assumed notes carry coupons of 8.375 to 9.625 percent and will keep interest above the pre-merger run-rate until they are retired or refinanced. Integration and operating execution still carry risk, with oil guidance lowered, rising unit lease operating costs and acquired-asset downtime. Off-debt commitments exist but are unquantified in part. Shareholder returns continue alongside deleveraging. The documentation behind the credit, including covenants, guarantors, indentures, ratings and a post-merger reserve base, is not in the sources.
